title: The Man Who Grew a Forest from Grief
shortDescription: A school-dropout in Assam watched floods leave snakes to die on a bare sandbar. Nothing, the forest department told him, would grow there. He spent decades proving them wrong — and still sells milk beside the forest he calls home.
introduction: The flood went away and left the snakes behind. They lay on the white sand of a Brahmaputra island, with not a tree to crawl under, and by afternoon they were dead. A teenage boy sat among them and wept. He was Jadav Payeng, of the Mising, an indigenous community of Assam whose life has always run with the river. When he asked the forest department whether anything could grow on that sandbar, they told him nothing would. So he asked the elders of a neighbouring village instead. They gave him bamboo. In 1979, on that bare sand, one boy's refusal to let grief be the end of the story became the beginning of a forest.

chapters.heading: What the river took
paragraphs: Before there was a forest, there was a river taking things away. Jadav Payeng was born on 31 October 1959 in Barghor, a Mising village in Jorhat district, Assam. He was the third of thirteen children of Lakhiram and Afuli Payeng. The Mising live by the Brahmaputra: they fish its channels, brew apong, a rice beer made with forest leaves, and build their houses knowing the water may come for them. Jadav grew up at Mohgorh Khuti, an old dockyard site that had once served the Jorehaut Provincial Railway. Between 1965 and 1970, the river ate ten kilometres of it. 'An erosion of 10 kilometres happened and Mohgorh Khuti turned into a desert,' he told The Hindu in 2020. He was a boy watching the ground under his feet disappear.

At five he was sent away to live with Anil Borthakur, a court-master at the Jorhat District Judge Court, so that he could go to school. He studied to Class X at Baligaon Jagannath Baruah Arya Vidyalaya. The family itself moved to Kokilamukh, on the river's north bank, where the erosion had followed them. He did not become a scholar. What stayed with him was the river's logic: it gave, then took. 'We Mishing people are connected to the river,' he said years later to Mongabay. 'The river's bounty has blessed us. But erosion caused by the river has posed a serious threat to our existence.' A town can retreat from a river. A village built on its edge cannot, not without becoming someone else.

This is the first thing to understand about the forest he later made. It was not a hobby or a campaign. It was an answer to a river that had emptied a place he loved. He had watched the Brahmaputra turn a dockyard into sand. When he found another stretch of sand years later, he did not see empty ground. He saw what the river had done, and he wondered whether a person could do the opposite. The question was still shapeless then. It needed a moment sharp enough to cut it into a decision. That moment came on a sandbar in the heat, among snakes that had nowhere to go.

chapters.heading: Nothing will grow there
paragraphs: In 1979, floodwater rose over the sandbar near Kokilamukh and, when it fell back, left snakes stranded on the bare sand. There was no shade. Jadav was in his teens. 'The snakes died in the heat, without any tree cover,' he told the Times of India in 2012. 'I sat down and wept over their lifeless forms. It was carnage.' He went to the forest department and asked whether trees could be grown there. The answer was no: nothing would grow on that sand. He was told to try bamboo instead. In a 2017 interview with NPR he put the whole moment in one sentence: 'In the grief of those dead snakes, I created this forest.'

The forest department could not tell him how. So he walked to a Deori village nearby — a community with its own knowledge of the river and its woods — and asked what would grow on a barren island. They gave him advice and planting material: fifty seeds and twenty-five bamboo saplings. He took what he was given to a place the experts had written off and planted it himself. Later a scientist named Jadabesh Barua gave him paan saplings and twenty-five paise, telling him to plant trees because they would take care of everyone. Small gifts, given by people who did not tell him to stop.

He asked a question no one had asked out loud: what would happen to people if they died like the snakes? 'I asked my elders what would happen if all of us died one day like those snakes,' he said in a 2026 interview. 'They laughed. But I knew I had to make the planet greener.' The laughter is worth keeping, because it is the sound of a reasonable person being told that grief is disproportionate. He had no land, no money and no authority. He had a few bamboo plants and a stretch of river sand. He began.

media.alt: Jadav Payeng seated on a large tree trunk in a Brahmaputra river sand bed
media.caption: Payeng on river sand of the kind he began planting on. Wikimedia Commons describes him sitting on a large trunk in the Brahmaputra's sand bed.

chapters.heading: A pot with holes in it
paragraphs: A sandbar is a hard place to keep anything alive. The sun burns, the water drains away, and floods come back without warning. Jadav worked out his own method. He cut bamboo platforms and set earthen pots with small holes above each sapling, so water dripped slowly for about a week. He mixed cow dung and organic matter into the soil, released earthworms into it, and used red ants to keep other insects away. 'I used cow dung and organic matter as manure to improve soil fertility,' he explained to Mongabay in 2018, 'to water the saplings, I employed an indigenous drip irrigation method that uses dripped earthen pots placed on bamboo platforms; and I also released earthworms to prepare the soil.' Nothing about it was grand. It was the kind of care a person gives when nobody is watching.

He had a living to make. Usually around half past three in the morning he milked the cows and buffaloes and washed them by eight. The milk went by boat to Jorhat, the nearest town. Then he rowed back, collected seedlings and walked out to the sandbar to tend them. There was no electricity in the house for years. The family moved three times as the river cut into the land again. In 1997 he married Binita; children came. Through all of it the planting continued, one sapling at a time, watered from a pot with holes in it.

This is where the story usually becomes a number — 550 hectares. But the number was built out of mornings like these. A pot filled. A hole checked. A sapling that had survived the week. 'People first thought I was crazy,' he told The Hindu. 'But I didn't give up on the saplings and came back every day to see their progress.' Craziness is a social judgement; progress is a daily one. He chose the daily one. The forest grew at the speed of a man walking out to check on a plant.

media.alt: Jadav Payeng standing among the trees of Molai Forest near Kokilamukh, Assam
media.caption: Payeng in the forest near Kokilamukh.
media.credit: JyotiPN / Wikimedia Commons — CC BY-SA 4.0 (image resized)

chapters.heading: The scheme ended. He stayed.
paragraphs: In 1980 the social forestry division of Golaghat district began a five-year plantation scheme on 200 hectares at Aruna Chapori, about five kilometres from Kokilamukh. Jadav was one of the labourers. The department supplied saplings; he learned the work on the government's ground and took its habits home with him. When the scheme ended, the other labourers left. He did not. 'Mulai was one of the labourers who worked in our project which was completed after five years,' the assistant conservator of forests Gunin Saikia later told PTI. 'He chose to stay back after the completion of the project as others left.'

Staying was a decision with no audience. There was no salary now, no delivery of saplings, no one to report to. He kept walking to the sandbar with seedlings and pots. He kept planting on ground that belonged to nobody in particular, in a river channel that could flood again. His family's milk money paid for the life around the work; the work itself paid nothing. He was the only person who kept turning up.

A person who keeps turning up becomes, slowly, a fact on the ground. Bamboo took hold first. Then taller trees: arjun, koroi, gamari, shimloo, shishoo, mango, jackfruit, neem, jamun, and more than a hundred recorded species. The sandbar stopped looking like a place the river had given up on. It began to look like a wood. He called it Molai Kathoni — Molai's woods — after the nickname his family used. It would be many years before anyone outside the district had a name for it.

chapters.heading: The men who came looking for elephants
paragraphs: In 2008 a herd of 115 elephants came out of the forest and damaged property at Aruna Chapori. Forest officials went looking for them and found the elephants inside something nobody in the department knew was there: a dense wood on a river sandbar. 'We were surprised to find such a dense forest on the sandbar,' Saikia told Mongabay. Once they found it, they found the man too. Saikia recognised Jadav as the labourer who had stayed on after the scheme. By then the plantation covered 550 hectares, about 1,360 acres, and it was home to deer, monkeys, birds and, increasingly, elephants.

The elephants did not repay him gently. The first herd destroyed his house. Villagers whose fields had been raided wanted to cut the forest down; Jadav dared them to kill him instead. He had made a home for wild animals on land that people also needed, and now the animals were eating what those people grew. His answer was not to blame the elephants. When around a hundred of his own cattle and buffaloes were lost to tigers over the years, he blamed the people who encroached on forests and destroyed them. 'Nature has made a food chain; why can't we stick to it?' he asked Mongabay in 2014. 'Who would protect these animals if we, as superior beings, start hunting them?'

Once, the family was eating lunch when a leopard dragged three buffaloes away. 'We don't interfere when wild animals take our livestock,' he told The Hindu. The losses were real. The forest was also real, and so was the argument it started. He had asked what would happen if people died like the snakes. Now people were telling him his answer had made their lives harder. He kept the forest. He also kept the milk, the cows and the small house inside the trees, and went on arguing with anyone who wanted to cut them down.

chapters.heading: Five gunshots in the rain
paragraphs: Making a forest is one thing. Keeping it is another. On 1 August 2012, Jadav heard five gunshots. He called the forest department and a local forest guard named Jitu Kalita. It was raining, and nobody went out that night. The carcass was found three days later: bullet holes, and the horn gone. The animal was a rhinoceros, one of the rare ones that had begun to use the forest. Sanctuary Asia recorded the night in detail; the men who should have gone did not, and the horn was not recovered. There is no triumph in the account. There is a man standing in the rain, telephoning, and an animal lying somewhere in the trees for three days.

It is a mistake to imagine Molai Kathoni as a sanctuary with gates. Jadav has called it a people's forest, a space shared by wildlife and humans. 'I've always envisaged Mulai Kathoni as a space to be shared by wildlife and humans,' he told Mongabay in 2018. In 2019 he asked the government to make it a community reserve, and asked for a boat and a forest outpost. 'I had asked for a boat and a forest outpost for Molai Kathoni. It's been years and am still waiting,' he said. The requests sound small beside 550 hectares. They are the difference between a forest that survives by one man's attention and one that has a legal name and a station.

Birds came back — the rufous treepie among them — and vultures after about twelve years. Deer, rabbits and monkeys arrived. By 2018, tigers and rhinos had been recorded in the forest, and elephants stayed for months at a time. He did not count the animals the way a report does. 'The birds, cows, deer, wind, water and elephants have helped me,' he told The Hindu. The gunshots were part of the same life as the birds. He kept both, and kept planting.

media.alt: A rufous treepie perched in Molai Forest near Jorhat, Assam
media.caption: A rufous treepie in Molai Forest. Birds were among the first signs that the sandbar had become a habitat.

chapters.heading: What he calls wealth
paragraphs: Recognition arrived late, and in a form he could carry. On 22 April 2012, at a public function at Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi, the vice-chancellor Sudhir Kumar Sopory called him the Forest Man of India. In 2015 the Government of India gave him a Padma Shri, one of the country's civilian honours; President Pranab Mukherjee conferred it at Rashtrapati Bhavan on 8 April. There were other honours — a Sanctuary Asia award in 2012, an honour from the Indian Institute of Forest Management in 2013, a Commonwealth Point of Light in 2020 — but the Padma is the one with a photograph: a man in a white shirt and shawl, holding a certificate, in a room very unlike a river sandbar.

Nothing about his days changed. He still lived in the forest, still sold milk, still walked among the trees. 'I have sacrificed everything and this jungle is my home now,' he said in 2026. 'The recognition and awards that I have received are my wealth, and that makes me the happiest man in the world.' There is a trap here — the rags-to-riches story wants a rich ending. He declined it. In 2017 he told a reporter that if each person planted a tree, there would be enough oxygen to arrest climate change. In 2022 he proposed a seven-day lockdown every year so the earth could recover. Both are the same idea as the pot with holes: small, repeated acts, offered by ordinary people.

A children's book now tells the story too: Jadav and the Tree-Place, written and illustrated by Vinayak Varma for Pratham Books' StoryWeaver. A documentary, Forest Man, took his message to a global audience, and he said the audience mattered more than the prize. 'People want to know my story. I tell them I just plant trees, and I'd like all of you to do so,' he told The Hindu. He offered no total, only the instruction.

media.caption: President Pranab Mukherjee presents the Padma Shri to Payeng at Rashtrapati Bhavan, New Delhi, on 8 April 2015.

chapters.heading: The fire, and the daughter
paragraphs: On 30 December 2025, someone set fire to Molai Kathoni 2.0, a newer planting near Baghmora eco-camp. More than 5,500 saplings that Jadav and his daughter Munmuni had planted in 2022 were destroyed, according to a forest official quoted by PTI. No one was hurt. Munmuni said fourteen of them went by mechanised boat and took nearly forty minutes to reach the fire. 'We used shrubs and branches with our hands, and fought the fire for a long time before it could be brought under control,' she said.

The daughter is the hinge of the ending. Munmuni now leads the work on Molai Kathoni 2.0, planting native, flood-resistant species. Jadav, in his sixties, still lives by the forest and still speaks about it. A man who once sat weeping over dead snakes now has a successor who fights fires with branches. The forest is bigger than any one person's life, which is what made it possible for one person to start it.

Go back to the sandbar. Snakes lay there in the heat because there was no shade. A boy wept, asked what would grow, was told nothing, and planted bamboo anyway. Nearly five decades later, the place has 550 hectares of trees, elephants and tigers, a photograph of a Padma ceremony, and a daughter beating out a fire with a branch. The boy's question was about dying. His answer took the form of shade. 'Every child should be asked to plant two trees,' he said in 2026. It is a small instruction for a very large answer — and it began with a pot with holes in it, dripping water onto one sapling that might not live.

sources.title: Meet Jadav Payeng, a man who created 550 hectares of forest single-handedly
sources.note: First-person interview. Supports the Mohgorh Khuti dockyard and the 1965–70 erosion that turned it into a desert; the small boat and daily return to saplings; people thinking he was crazy; Jadabesh Barua's paan saplings and 25 paise; the leopard taking three buffaloes at lunch and 'We don't interfere'; 'The birds, cows, deer, wind, water and elephants have helped me'; and 'I just plant trees, and I'd like all of you to do so.'

sources.title: The man who made a forest
sources.note: Canonical 1979 account: snakes washed onto a treeless sandbar, dying in the heat; 'I sat down and wept over their lifeless forms. It was carnage'; the forest department saying nothing would grow and suggesting bamboo; 'There was nobody to help me. Nobody was interested.'

sources.title: 'I'd take his own life before killing a tree': meet India's forest man
sources.note: International profile. Supports 'When I saw it, I thought even we humans will have to die this way in the heat' and 'In the grief of those dead snakes, I created this forest.'

sources.title: One man plants forest larger than Central Park
sources.note: Field report. Supports the 550-hectare / 1,360-acre figure; the 2008 forest-department search for 115 elephants and Gunin Saikia's recognition; villagers wanting to cut the forest and Payeng daring them to kill him; about 100 cattle and buffaloes lost to tigers; and the food-chain and hunting quotations.

sources.title: Can India's peoples' forest also serve as a haven for rhinos?
sources.note: Supports the earthen-pot drip method, cow dung, earthworms and red ants; the Mishing-river quotation; 'I've always envisaged Mulai Kathoni as a space to be shared by wildlife and humans'; the 2019-style request framing and the community-reserve wish; and the 2018 rhino and tiger reports.

sources.title: The strange obsession of Jadav Payeng
sources.note: Supports the 3:30 a.m. milking routine, bathing livestock by eight, rowing milk to Jorhat, no electricity, houses moved three times; the first elephant herd destroying his home; the 1 August 2012 five gunshots, the rain, the guarded carcass found three days later with its horn missing; and the Mising context.

sources.title: Man creates forest single-handedly on Brahmaputra sand bar (PTI)
sources.publisher: Asian Age / Press Trust of India (archived)
sources.note: Supports the 1980 Golaghat social-forestry scheme on 200 hectares at Aruna Chapori, the five-year completion, Gunin Saikia's 'He chose to stay back after the completion of the project as others left', and the 2008 elephant-search discovery.

sources.title: Jadav Payeng correspondence, Current Science 106(4), p.499
sources.note: Peer-reviewed correspondence. Supports the 1979/1980 dating, the species list including arjun, koroi, gamari, shimloo, shishoo, mango, jackfruit, neem and jamun, red ants, and the JNU 22 April 2012 'Forest Man of India' title conferred by vice-chancellor Sudhir Kumar Sopory.

sources.title: The man who planted a forest — interview
sources.note: Supports the Deori village visit, the snakes 'writhing and dying under the hot sun', and the fifty seeds and twenty-five bamboo saplings given to him.

sources.title: World's first man-made forest: a conversation with Jadav Payeng
sources.note: First-person account. Supports the 31 October 1959 birth, father Lakhiram, mother Afuli, third of thirteen children, the Barghor village, fifty bamboo heads and twenty-five stalks, and Deori advice about planting the tallest grass in the world. The 'world's first man-made forest' headline is not used as fact.

sources.title: The call of the forest man
sources.note: Supports the drip-irrigation pots, soil improvement, and 'If each man plants a tree we will have enough oxygen to arrest climate change.' Its '1,360 hectares' figure is a unit error; the dominant figure is 1,360 acres / 550 hectares.

sources.title: Eco Hero: Jadav Payeng
sources.note: Supports the palm-reader anecdote, 'My jungle is my wealth and I am a happy man', and the 1978 dating variant, which is noted in the sources rather than treated as settled.

sources.title: Forest maker: Jadav Payeng
sources.note: Supports being left at five with court-master Anil Borthakur, schooling at Baligaon Jagannath Baruah Arya Vidyalaya to Class X, and the family's Kokilamukh location.

sources.title: Local legends: meet Padma Shri awardee Jadav Payeng
sources.note: Supports 'I asked my elders what would happen if all of us died one day like those snakes. They laughed. But I knew I had to make the planet greener'; 'I have sacrificed everything and this jungle is my home now'; 'The recognition and awards that I have received are my wealth'; 'Every child should be asked to plant two trees'; his living status in 2026; and the daughter-led Molai Kathoni 2.0. Its 1963 birth year conflicts with his own 1959 account; its million-sapling figure is single-source and hedged in the prose.

sources.title: Miscreants set afire forest created by 'Forest Man of India' in Assam (PTI)
sources.note: Supports the 30 December 2025 fire at Molai Kathoni 2.0, more than 5,500 saplings planted in 2022 destroyed per a forest official, no human casualty, and Munmuni Payeng's account of fourteen people rowing nearly forty minutes and fighting the fire with shrubs and branches. Sand-mining allegations were political claims and are not stated as findings.

sources.title: India's 'Forest Man' Jadav Payeng on a Mexico mission to plant trees
sources.note: Reports the 2021 Fundación Azteca invitation and a seven-million-tree target. The target is not narrated as completed.

sources.title: Only man cuts others, grow the forest: Forest Man of India on healing the planet
sources.note: Supports the 2022 proposal of a seven-day lockdown every year so the earth can recover: 'We should call for a seven-day lockdown every year so that Earth gets time to recover from the damage we do.' The page blocked direct fetching; the quotation was recovered from indexed search text.

sources.title: India's forest man wants Assam's erosion-prone Molai woods to become a community reserve
sources.note: Supports the 2019 request for community-reserve status and 'I had asked for a boat and a forest outpost for Molai Kathoni. It's been years and am still waiting.' The headline's 'world's largest man-made forest' claim is not used in the story.

sources.title: Jadav and the Tree-Place
sources.note: Children's book written and illustrated by Vinayak Varma, used in the closing chapter.

sources.title: Man plants forest, becomes film star
sources.note: Supports the documentary Forest Man by William Douglas McMaster, its 2014 Cannes Emerging Filmmakers showcase, and Payeng's quoted view that the global audience mattered more than the award.
